778.title: His family carried the dead cattle
778.hook: Ravidas sings that his family carried dead animals near Benares, yet great men bow to him now (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)
778.howItsDone: Sikhs hear these hymns of Ravidas in the gurdwara as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Sikh ideal of kirat karni, honest work, honors labor of every kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gareeb nivaaj: the one who cherishes the poor, holding a king's canopy over a leather-worker's head. Today, Ravidas names his family's trade out loud.

Before dawn, a truck stops outside, and someone you'll never meet carries off your trash. A worker in a hospital basement washes what nobody wants to wash. Somewhere, a person handles the dead so the rest of us don't have to. These jobs get noticed mostly by their absence, the day they aren't done. In Raag Malar, Ravidas opens a hymn by addressing the whole town and naming his family's work. Not hinting at it. Naming it.
screen: `THE TRUCK BEFORE DAWN.` → `JOBS WE KNOW BY THEIR ABSENCE.` → `RAVIDAS NAMES HIS FAMILY'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Two hymns sit side by side on Ang 1293 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Four days ago this path heard the second, with the learned bowing. Today, start with the first. It opens, in paraphrase: people of the town, my caste is well known; it is the leather-workers' caste. And in my heart I hold the Lord's virtues. Then a picture from a scribe's desk. The palm tree is counted impure, and so is the paper made from its leaves. But when the Lord's praise is written on that paper, people bow before it and worship it. The material doesn't change. What's written on it changes how it's treated. Ravidas sets himself right there: the same family, the same trade, and the Name written into him. The second hymn adds one small word that carries a lot: still. His relatives, he says, still go around Benares hauling away dead cattle. He doesn't say they used to, or that he got out, so the honor can't be explained by escape. Brahmins of careful conduct bow before him anyway, and he calls himself the servant of the Lord's servants. In that same hymn he names Kabir too, as if to say: the Lord keeps doing this. He doesn't ask to be reclassified, or call the work beneath him. Sikh teaching has a name for honest work: kirat karni, earning by your own labor. So today's line, every job is holy, isn't Ravidas's exact phrase. It's what his song does: it names a job the town shrank from, right at the top, and doesn't apologize.
screen: `PEOPLE OF THE TOWN, MY CASTE IS KNOWN.` · `PALM-LEAF PAPER, BOWED TO WHEN IT HOLDS PRAISE.` · `STILL HAULING DEAD CATTLE IN BENARES.` · then, large: `NO APOLOGY FOR THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Trace something you touched today back to the hands that dealt with its mess: the drain, the bin, the floor, the laundry, the shoes. Let one of those workers come to mind, even without a face, and stay with them a few breaths, without pity, the way Ravidas stays with his family's work. Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.
Kirat karni. Sikh teaching's name for earning by your own labor: Ravidas naming his family's trade before the whole town, and not apologizing for it.
Your line: every job is holy. Someone's hard work is holding up your day. See you tomorrow.

779.title: Ravidas close
779.hook: Ravidas is honored by Sikhs, and by the Ravidassia community, who hold him especially dear
779.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Ravidas's hymns in the gurdwara as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, while the Ravidassia community honors him as Guru Ravidas in its own gatherings and celebrates his birthday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat karni: Ravidas naming his family's trade to the whole town, and the learned bowing anyway. Today, the last of the Ravidas days.

Two buildings, maybe on the same street. In one, a gurdwara, Sikhs sing a hymn of Ravidas from the Guru Granth Sahib. In the other, members of the Ravidassia community gather under his picture and call him Guru Ravidas. Same man. Same songs. Two communities who honor him, each in its own way. Today closes the Ravidas days with a question: what does it mean to honor a saint who is someone else's too?
screen: `TWO BUILDINGS, ONE NAME.` → `SIKHS SING HIS HYMNS.` → `THE RAVIDASSIA CALL HIM GURU.`

segments.voice: First, a look back. The shoemaker of Benares, a leather-worker whose family were counted low. Begampura, his city without sorrow, with no tax and no fear, where all walk free. Sandalwood and castor: the plain plant made fragrant by standing close. Who but You: the king's canopy over his head. And yesterday, his family still hauling dead cattle while the learned bow. Five pictures, one voice. Now, who keeps that voice? For Sikhs, Ravidas is a Bhagat, a devotee, and his hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib. In the gurdwara they're sung with the same reverence as the Gurus' own words, and when they're read, the whole book is honored, not one author over another. For the Ravidassia community, Ravidas is their Guru, and he stands at the center. They have their own places of worship, and his birthday is a great day for them. The two communities share a great deal and differ on some things, and each tells its own story about how they relate. This path won't settle that, and doesn't need to. What it can say is that the songs don't belong to one fence. Begampura is a city where all walk free; that song keeps opening the gate. And one plain fact stands: the man whose touch his town called polluting is now honored by more than one community, and not all in the same words. His song is big enough for that.
screen: `FIVE PICTURES, ONE VOICE.` · `FOR SIKHS: A BHAGAT IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · `FOR THE RAVIDASSIA: THEIR GURU.` · then, large: `A SONG BIGGER THAN ONE FENCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a holy figure who belongs to someone you know, but isn't yours, or isn't yours in the same way: a coworker's saint, a friend's teacher, a neighbor's guru. Hold their name with respect, the way you'd want yours held, and if you know nothing about them, let that honest not-knowing be where you start. If you pray, you can breathe out with Waheguru.
Bhagat. A devotee whose hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib: Ravidas, a Bhagat for Sikhs and Guru Ravidas for the Ravidassia, one song for both.
Your line: his song for all. One singer, more than one home. That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Trilochan: the last thought
780.hook: what we think of at the very end shapes where we go (Gujri, Trilochan, ang 526)
780.howItsDone: Trilochan's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs traditionally end the day with Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and simran, remembering the Name before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat: a leather-worker's songs, kept by Sikhs and by the Ravidassia, a song for all. Today, a new Bhagat, and a hard question.

What was on your mind just before you fell asleep last night? A bill. A message you shouldn't have sent. Tomorrow's meeting. A face. Sometimes that thought is still there in the morning. Trilochan's hymn is about that last thought, stretched to its limit: not the last thought before sleep, but the last one at the very end of a life.
screen: `THE THOUGHT BEFORE SLEEP.` → `STILL THERE IN THE MORNING.` → `TRILOCHAN: THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: Trilochan is one of the devotees Ravidas named three days ago, and today he gets his own hymn, in Raag Gujri, on Ang 526 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Its refrain, the line it keeps coming back to, is a plea to a sister, in paraphrase: O sister, don't forget the Name of Gobind. Then he builds a ladder of pictures, each in the same frame. At the last moment, whoever thinks of wealth, and dies in that thought, is born again and again as a serpent, coiled around the treasure, you might say. Whoever thinks of sons and family is born as a pig, nosing among a crowd of young. Whoever thinks of mansions dies and wanders like a ghost, haunting the halls. Each picture is the thought made into a body: in the hymn, what a person holds onto at the end, they become. Then the last verse turns. Whoever, at the last moment, thinks of the Lord and dies in that thought is set free, and the Lord, the hymn says, dwells in that heart. It's a warning. Many readers also hear something practical in it: the thought that shows up at the end is likely the one that's been showing up all along, at red lights, in the shower, at two in the morning. That's why the refrain isn't about dying. It's about not forgetting, today. In the Sikh telling, the Name is remembered through simran, steady remembrance. The pictures are strange, even a little grim, but the plea underneath is gentle: sister, don't forget.
screen: `O SISTER, DON'T FORGET THE NAME.` · `WEALTH, FAMILY, MANSIONS: THE THOUGHT BECOMES A BODY.` · `THE LORD AT THE END: SET FREE.` · then, large: `THE LAST THOUGHT IS PRACTICED NOW.`

segments.voice: Choose a good thought to end today with, while it's easy: a face you love, a line from this path, a moment you're grateful for, or, if you pray, the Name. Say it to yourself slowly, until it's short enough to find in the dark. Then rest with it, breathing out Waheguru if that's yours.

Your line: the last thought. It's being practiced right now. Day seven hundred eighty, done.

781.title: Beni: the stages of life
781.hook: Beni traces a life from the womb to old age, forgetting the Lord at each stage (Sri Rag, Beni, ang 93)
781.howItsDone: Beni's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching speaks of jivan mukti, being free while still alive, through remembering the Name in everyday life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trilochan: the last thought, and a plea to a sister not to forget the Name. Today, another Bhagat looks at a whole life.

A box of family photos, tipped out on a table. A baby in a hospital blanket. A kid with a scraped knee and a grin. A teenager trying hard to look bored. A wedding. A gray head bent over a grandchild. Shuffle them into order and you have a whole life in a few minutes. Beni, one of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib, lays out a life like that in a hymn, from the womb to old age. And in every snapshot, something is missing.
screen: `A BOX OF PHOTOS ON THE TABLE.` → `A WHOLE LIFE IN ORDER.` → `IN EVERY ONE, SOMETHING MISSING.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Sri Raag, on Ang 93, and it starts somewhere surprising: before birth. In paraphrase: O man, when you were in the womb, upside down, you were absorbed in remembering, with no pride in your body. Then you were born, and you forgot. Next, childhood: caught up in play and sweets, the Lord slips from mind. Then youth: the body is strong, the eye wanders after pleasure and money, and pride grows. Then old age: the hair goes white, the body weakens, and there's regret, but now it's hard to change course. Each stage has its own reason to forget. The child is too busy. The young adult is too sure. The old one is too tired. Beni isn't mocking any of them. Forgetting doesn't belong to one bad season of life; it comes along to every one. Then he signs off with a hard question, in paraphrase: says Beni, listen, devotees, who has ever found liberation after death? That's the turn. If freedom doesn't come after death, it has to come in one of these photos. Sikh teaching speaks of being free while still alive, here, in the middle of an ordinary life. Read that way, the hymn points to the photo you're in right now, the stage you're standing in, with its own reason to forget, as the place to remember.
screen: `IN THE WOMB, REMEMBERING.` · `CHILD, YOUTH, OLD AGE: EACH ONE FORGETS.` · `WHO IS FREED AFTER DEATH?` · then, large: `THE STAGE YOU'RE IN NOW.`

segments.voice: Find yourself in Beni's photos: busy like the child, sure like the young, tired like the old, or somewhere between. Name your stage's own reason to forget, honestly and without blame, and then just breathe, remembering right where you are. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath.
Beni. The Bhagat of Sri Raag who lays out a life from the womb to old age, finds forgetting in every stage, and asks who was ever freed after death.
Your line: remember at every stage. Every stage has room for it, this one included. Seven hundred eighty-one days now.

782.title: Dhanna the farmer
782.hook: Dhanna prays plainly for flour, lentils, ghee, a cow and a good wife (Dhanasri, Dhanna, ang 695)
782.howItsDone: Dhanna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bring ordinary needs as well as spiritual ones into ardas, the standing prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Beni: the photos of a life, and a reason to forget in every one. Today, a farmer prays without dressing it up.

O Gopal, I'm a beggar at Your door. That's how one hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib begins, in paraphrase, and what follows sounds less like poetry than a shopping list. It sits between hymns about the soul and the Infinite. It belongs to Dhanna, a farmer, and it's addressed straight to God. He doesn't dress it up or explain himself. He stands at the door and asks for groceries.
screen: `O GOPAL, A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR.` → `BETWEEN HYMNS OF THE SOUL, A LIST.` → `DHANNA ASKS FOR GROCERIES.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695. It opens with the word aarta. Some read it as one in need, a beggar at the door; others hear in it aarti, an offering of worship. In paraphrase: O Gopal, Sustainer of the world, I'm a beggar at Your door; You take care of the work of those devoted to You. Then the list. Lentils, flour and ghee, so my heart can be content each day. Shoes, and good clothes. Grain. A cow and a buffalo that give milk. A fine horse. And a good wife to keep the home. The last line: your servant Dhanna asks for these. No apology, no explanation that what he really wants is something higher. Look at the kind of things they are: food for the table, something on the feet, animals that keep a farm alive, a partner. It's the list of a working household, said out loud to the Lord, as if the Lord were the one who could be asked. And it stands in the Guru's book, beside songs of longing for the Lord. Some people feel a prayer has to be cleaned up first: made noble, made about other people, the part about rent hidden. Dhanna's hymn quietly says the plain thing is allowed. Trust shows up in the asking. Tradition tells other stories about Dhanna, about a stone and a simple farmer's faith; those can wait for another day. Today it's the list, and the man who wasn't embarrassed to say it to God.

If you pray, offer it plainly, as Dhanna did, someone asking at a door; if you don't, simply hold it honestly as a need. Then let it go out with the breath, with Waheguru if you like.

783.title: Sain the barber
783.hook: Sain's aarti offers incense, lamp and ghee, then his whole self (Dhanasri, Sain, ang 695)
783.howItsDone: Sain's aarti is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching counts honest work, kirat, as part of a devoted life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarta: lentils, flour and a cow, asked for plainly at the Lord's door. Today, on the same page, a barber lights a lamp.

How close do you let a stranger come to your face with a blade? A barber's day is small, careful movements an inch from someone's throat. Trust is the whole job. Tradition remembers Sain as a barber, and on the same page of the Guru Granth Sahib as Dhanna's grocery list, he left a hymn of worship: an aarti, the lamp ceremony, with incense and flame. But by the end, what he offers isn't on the tray.
screen: `A BLADE NEAR THE FACE.` → `A BARBER'S CAREFUL HANDS.` → `AN AARTI ON THE SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: Aarti, in Indian worship, is the waving of a lamp before the divine, often with incense and a lamp fed with ghee, clarified butter. Sain's hymn, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, opens right there. In paraphrase: with incense, lamp and ghee I make ready the aarti. And in the next breath: I am a sacrifice to the Lord. Vaarne jaau, in the Gurmukhi: I give myself over. The tray is set, but the offering is the person holding it. The refrain is pure celebration: joy to the Lord, joy every day to the Sovereign King. Then Sain looks at the lamp again. The finest lamp, the purest wick, he sings, and turns to the Lord: You are the Immaculate One. As if the true flame isn't the one in his hand. Then a surprise: he names a teacher. Ramanand, he says, knows the devotion of the Lord, and speaks of the Lord as perfect, supreme bliss. Ramanand's own hymn comes in a few days. The close: worship the Lord, the supreme bliss, who carries you across the frightening sea. Tradition tells a story about Sain, retold by the Sikh poet Bhai Gurdas: once he stayed so long with holy people that he missed his duty at the king's court, and the Lord came in his form and served the king in his place. Whatever you make of the story, it fits the hymn: the barber's work and the barber's worship are one offering.
screen: `INCENSE, LAMP AND GHEE.` · `VAARNE JAAU: I GIVE MYSELF.` · `YOU ARE THE TRUE FLAME.` · then, large: `THE WORK AND THE WORSHIP, ONE OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Picture what your hands will do today, emails, meals, a shift, a diaper, a classroom, and see its tools the way Sain had scissors and comb. Quietly offer the work itself, done carefully, as your aarti, whether you call it that or not. If you pray, let Waheguru ride each breath out.
Aarti. The lamp ceremony of worship, incense and ghee on the tray, until Sain turns himself into the offering: I am a sacrifice to the Lord.
Your line: the barber's aarti. Scissors and comb belong on the tray too. That's day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: Pipa the king
784.hook: a king turned devotee sings that the body itself is the temple (Dhanasri, Pipa, ang 695)
784.howItsDone: Pipa's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, on the same page as the hymns of Dhanna and Sain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarti: incense, lamp and ghee, and then Sain himself as the offering. Today, a king moves the whole tray somewhere closer.

A king has everything a temple needs: money for the marble, priests on the payroll, gold for the lamps. Tradition says Pipa was a king like that, who left his throne to follow the path of devotion. So when he sings about where God is worshipped, you might expect a grand building. Instead, on the same page as Dhanna and Sain, Pipa points somewhere much closer. It's been with you all day. It's breathing right now.
screen: `MARBLE, PRIESTS, GOLD LAMPS.` → `A KING WHO LEFT THE THRONE.` → `HE POINTS SOMEWHERE CLOSER.`

segments.voice: Pipa's hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695, and its key word is kaaiaa, the body. In paraphrase, it opens: the body is the deity, the body is the temple, the body is the pilgrim. Within the body are the incense, the lamp and the offerings of food, and the leaves laid down in worship. Hear it next to yesterday. Sain set out incense, lamp and ghee on the tray, then offered himself. Pipa takes the whole tray and moves it inside: temple, pilgrim, lamp and offering, all found in the body. Then a search. In paraphrase: I searched through many realms, and found the treasures within the body. Nothing comes and nothing goes. And a line worth holding onto: what is in the universe is in the body; whoever searches, finds. The hymn closes: Pipa prays, the supreme essence is there, and the True Guru reveals it. Two things to notice. This isn't about the body as something to perfect or show off. It's the place where the sacred is met, the ordinary one, tired or sick or young or old. And it isn't a do-it-yourself map: Pipa ends with the True Guru, the one who shows you what was there all along. A king who could have paid for any temple, saying: the temple was here.
screen: `KAAIAA: THE BODY.` · `DEITY, TEMPLE, PILGRIM, LAMP: ALL WITHIN.` · `WHAT'S IN THE UNIVERSE IS IN THE BODY.` · then, large: `THE TRUE GURU SHOWS IT.`

segments.voice: Walk through your body gently, the way a pilgrim walks into a holy place: the feet that carried you here, the hands that worked, the chest rising and falling. Whatever aches, let it be part of the temple too, without judging it. If you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe out.
Kaaiaa. Pipa's word for the body: the deity, the temple and the pilgrim all found within it, with the True Guru showing what's there.
Your line: the body is the temple. The week went from dead cattle to a farmer's list, a barber's lamp and a king's temple. Day seven hundred eighty-four, done.
